forces: Two four-part choirs and two orchestras, with a soprano ripieno choir
performers: Münchener Bach-Chor and Münchener Chorknaben; Münchener Bach-Orchester; Karl Richter, conductor
intro: Karl Richter conducts “Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen”, the opening chorus of Bach’s St Matthew Passion, BWV 244, in this 1958 recording. Two choirs alternate in E minor, and a third group of singers sings a hymn melody above them.

sections.label: Intro · Two orchestras over a rocking bass
sections.mNote: Flutes, oboes and strings play before the choirs enter.

sections.label: A · First choir: “Kommt, ihr Töchter”
sections.mNote: “Kommt, ihr Töchter” opens a dialogue between the two choirs.

sections.label: B · Hymn above the dialogue
sections.mNote: The ripieno sopranos sing O Lamm Gottes in long notes.

sections.label: C · The wood of the cross
sections.mNote: The choirs sing the last lines of the poem.

sections.label: A′ · Return of “Kommt, ihr Töchter”
sections.mNote: The opening words return after the chorale ends.

cues.title: Instrumental introduction, two orchestras
cues.text: E repeats in the bass beneath groups of three notes. Two orchestras play together, each with flutes, oboes, strings and continuo. The instruments play alone for sixteen bars in E minor before the voices enter.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, vol. 4 (1854), Part I, printed pp. 1–4: 12/8 introduction in E minor, instrumental staves marked Coro I. II. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/62/IMSLP00934-Bach_StMatt1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Picander’s libretto, 1727
cues.text: Picander, the pen name of Christian Friedrich Henrici, assigned this chorus to the Daughters of Zion and the faithful. One group calls and the other asks questions. Bach gave each group its own choir and orchestra, so the dialogue passes between two bodies of singers.
cues.evidence: Picander’s libretto for BWV 244, Leipzig, 1727; explanation of the two groups and Bach’s two ensembles: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244.

cues.title: Entry of the first choir
cues.text: “Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen” — “Come, daughters, help me mourn.” The first choir enters in four parts. The second choir and its orchestra rest, and the first orchestra accompanies the voices over the repeated bass.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 4–5, bar 17 onwards: Choir I enters, with Choir II and Orchestra II resting. Picander’s opening text, Leipzig, 1727.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Karl Richter’s recording, 1958
cues.text: Karl Richter recorded the Passion in stereo, then a new process, over twenty-two sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958, some of them running late into the night. Critics first remarked on his speed. One wrote that Klemperer’s recording lasted about forty minutes longer.
cues.evidence: Deutsche Grammophon booklet for the 1958 recording (Internet Archive item, Booklet.pdf): 22 sessions, 23 June to 21 August 1958, stereo; Renate Freyse in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik on the length of Klemperer’s recording. https://archive.org/details/munchener-bach-chor-munchener-bach-orchester-karl-richter-johann-sebastian-b

cues.title: Entry of the ripieno sopranos
cues.text: The ripieno sopranos enter with “O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig” — “O Lamb of God, innocent”. Their hymn in G major moves in long notes above the two choirs and the instruments. Beneath it the first choir starts “Kommt, ihr Töchter” again, and the second choir goes on with its short questions.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 7 onwards: Soprano ripieno enters at bar 30. The G-major chorale above E-minor music is discussed by Martin Pearlman: https://baroque.boston/js-bach-st-matthew-passion. Hymn text printed in the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chorale “O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig”
cues.text: The boys sing “O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig”, a German version of the Agnus Dei by Nikolaus Decius, a monastery provost who left his cloister for the Reformation in 1522. It was first printed in 1531, in a Low German hymnbook from Rostock. The tune is set in long notes above both choirs.
cues.evidence: John Julian, A Dictionary of Hymnology (1892), “O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig”: the Low German text is in Geystliche leder (Rostock, 1531), the High German in Valentin Schumann’s hymnbook (Leipzig, 1539): https://hymnology.hymnsam.co.uk/o/o-lamm-gottes,-unschuldig. Julian’s life of Decius, as reprinted at Hymnary.org (he left Steterburg in July 1522): https://hymnary.org/tune/o_lamm_gottes_unschuldig_decius. Its use as cantus firmus in the opening chorus: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 7 onwards.

cues.title: Autograph score, 1736
cues.text: In 1736 Bach prepared a careful new score of the Passion, now in the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, and wrote the words of the Gospel in red ink. He also wrote the words and notes of this opening hymn in red, above the two choirs.
cues.evidence: Bach’s 1736 autograph, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 25. Red ink for the biblical text and the opening chorale: Martin Pearlman, https://baroque.boston/js-bach-st-matthew-passion.

cues.title: Funeral music for Prince Leopold, 1729
cues.text: In March 1729 Bach wrote funeral music for his former employer, Prince Leopold. Ten of its movements were derived from, or served as models for, music in the Passion. Picander wrote the words for both.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society, notes on BWV 244: ten movements of the funeral music for Prince Leopold, written for the service of March 1729, are derived from or modelled on the Passion. https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244. The funeral music (BWV 244a, first performed at Köthen on 23–24 March 1729) has words by Picander (Christian Friedrich Henrici): https://www.bach-cantatas.com/BWV244a.htm

cues.title: St Matthew Passion, Leipzig, 1727
cues.text: On Good Friday, 11 April 1727, Bach performed the St Matthew Passion at vespers in St Thomas’s Church, Leipzig. He had been the city’s Thomaskantor for four years. Leipzig had heard his St John Passion in 1724.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1723, 1724 and 1727: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. Occasion and church: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244.

cues.title: Final lines and chorale plea
cues.text: The two choirs sing of Jesus carrying the wood of the cross himself, “aus Lieb und Huld” (“out of love and grace”). After the short questions, they now set the words in longer groups. Above them, the chorale reaches its final line: “Have mercy on us, O Jesus.”
cues.evidence: Picander’s final lines and the chorale’s Erbarm dich unser, o Jesu, Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 17–19. Complete text: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Berlin performances, March 1829
cues.text: On 11 March 1829 the twenty-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted the Passion with the Berlin Singakademie, with Eduard Devrient singing Christ. Most of the arias were left out. A second performance on 21 March was as crowded as the first, and the takings went to a sewing school for poor girls.
cues.evidence: Eduard Devrient, who sang Christ, in My Recollections of Felix Mendelssohn-Bartholdy and His Letters to Me, trans. Natalia Macfarren (London, 1869), pp. 56 and 61–63: the performance of 11 March 1829; “Most of the songs would have to be omitted”; the second performance on 21 March, “crowded like the first”; the proceeds for a sewing school for poor girls. https://archive.org/details/bwb_P9-BTS-586

cues.title: Return of the opening text
cues.text: After the hymn, the two main choirs sing “Kommt, ihr Töchter” again (bars 82–90). A B pedal in the bass holds the music on the dominant of E minor. Both choirs join on “als wie ein Lamm” — “like a lamb” — before the cadence in E minor.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 20–21, bars 82–90: returning opening text over a B pedal, final words and E-minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Choir I enters at bar 17
transitions.from: Intro · Two orchestras over a rocking bass
transitions.how: The E-minor introduction leads straight into the first choir’s entry at bar 17. Choir I sings “Kommt, ihr Töchter”, and Orchestra II stops playing. The first orchestra continues the 12/8 figures and the repeated bass under the four vocal parts. The second choir rests.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, vol. 4 (1854), Part I, printed p. 4: bar 17, Choir I entry and rests in Coro II.

transitions.title: Chorale entry above the two choirs
transitions.how: The ripieno sopranos enter with “O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig”, a G-major hymn in long notes above the E-minor music. Choir I returns to its opening words and Choir II has short questions. The orchestras continue underneath. The bass keeps its lilting rhythm while the new melody spans whole bars.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 7, bar 30 onwards: chorale entry. G-major hymn within the E-minor movement: Martin Pearlman, https://baroque.boston/js-bach-st-matthew-passion.

transitions.title: The final lines of Picander’s text
transitions.to: C · The wood of the cross
transitions.how: The short questions give way to the poem’s last sentence, about Jesus carrying the cross himself. Each choir sings in larger blocks, supported by its own orchestra. The continuo keeps moving beneath them while the ripieno sopranos finish their hymn with “Erbarm dich unser, o Jesu”.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 17–19: final lines of Picander’s text in the two choirs and final phrase of the ripieno chorale.

transitions.title: The opening words over low B
transitions.from: C · The wood of the cross
transitions.how: The hymn has finished. The two choirs return to “Kommt, ihr Töchter” in bars 82–90, above repeated B in the continuo, the dominant of E minor. Flutes, oboes and strings continue their winding lines. The bass then moves from B to E for the closing E-minor cadence, and the choirs come together on the last words, “als wie ein Lamm”.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 20–21, bars 82–90: returning opening words, B pedal and closing E-minor cadence.

source.title: Bach, Passionsmusik nach dem Evangelisten Matthäus (Matthäus-Passion), BWV 244, Bach-Gesellschaft Ausgabe, vol. 4, Erster Theil (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854)
source.locator: No. 1, printed pp. 1–21: two choirs and two orchestras, each with two flutes, two oboes, strings and continuo. The separate Soprano ripieno staff carries O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig. Orchestra II rests at Choir I’s first entry.

timeline.note: Both orchestras play the rocking 12/8 figures above repeated bass notes. None of the three groups of singers has yet entered.
Choir I begins Kommt, ihr Töchter with its own orchestra. Choir II and Orchestra II rest.
Choir II asks Wen? and Wie? in short phrases; Choir I answers.
The ripieno sopranos begin O Lamm Gottes in long notes above the choirs and orchestras.
Choir II asks “Was?” and “Wohin?” while Choir I answers and the ripieno sopranos continue the hymn.
The two choirs sing the poem’s last lines as the ripieno sopranos reach Erbarm dich unser, o Jesu.
The ripieno sopranos have finished. The main choirs return to the opening words and close together in E minor.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Münchener Bach-Chor (chorus (Chorus I and II)), Münchener Chorknaben (boys’ choir, ripieno soprano (chorale ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’)), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor)
fields.note: The booklet track list gives the chorale to the Knabenchor. The booklet also names instrumental soloists for the whole Passion (flutes Walther Theurer and Wolfgang Haag; oboes Edgar Shann and Kurt Hausmann; organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl), and Fritz Rothschuh as chorus master. Their assignment to this number is not stated, so they are not listed as performers of it.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736, and cites the autograph score Mus. ms. Bach P 25 and the parts St 110. The booklet and the Bach-Gesellschaft score number this chorus No. 1; the New Bach Edition also numbers it 1.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August)
fields.note: The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958 and its credit line gives 6–8/1958. Which session produced No. 1 is not stated.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Archiv Produktion (Deutsche Grammophon Gesellschaft, History of Music Division)
fields.note: The labels read ‘Archive Production — History of Music Division Deutsche Grammophon Ges.’ and ‘Stereo’.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: SAPM 198 009/012 (first stereo edition, four LPs); the scanned export pressing carries ARC 73 125–73 128 / SAPM 198 625–628
fields.note: First release year is disputed in the sources: the booklet and Wikipedia say 1959 (the booklet reads ‘LPs released/veröffentlicht/paru 1959’ and prints ℗ 1959 Deutsche Grammophon); Discogs and the Internet Archive LP catalogue give 1958, which is the recording year. Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: First stereo edition: first programme side of the set (Discogs side A), first track (9:50 on the LP); matrix and take numbers not read
fields.note: The side and position come from the Discogs tracklist only, whose first edition is automatically coupled, so the programme side is not the physical side of a particular LP. No run-out inscription was seen, so matrix and take are unknown.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No remastering engineer or studio is credited in the item metadata or the booklet. The booklet’s © 2001 Deutsche Grammophon notice and the retail page’s ‘Digitally remastered’ line show only that commercial digital releases exist. The upload is a private Internet Archive upload in the hifidelity collection.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The Internet Archive item was created on 16 February 2026; that upload date is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: 24-bit/192 kHz FLAC (item description ‘1959 [FLAC 24-192]’), digitally remastered according to the retail page; streamed here through the Internet Archive’s VBR MP3 derivative.
fields.note: The item’s track titles and durations (9:49 for this track) match the retail page’s 2016 hi-res listing, so the file is probably that release, but the item names no source. No speed correction, noise reduction or restoration settings are stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Bach’s composition (d. 1750) and the Bach-Gesellschaft edition used for the orchestra view (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854) are public domain.
fields.note: IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959).
fields.note: Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
